corrections.issue: Speakers are merged. The observation that the industry never discusses 1980s-90s crises and starts crisis alpha with the tech bubble is the host's (Niels); the list of upheavals (Plaza Accord, S&L collapse, dollar overshoot, 1987 crash, Soros and the Bank of England, Latin American and Tequila crises) is Mark's, and Niels adds the 1998 Asian crisis.
corrections.fix: Mark Rzepczynski lists 1980s-90s upheavals (Plaza Accord, S&L failures, dollar overshoot, 1987 crash, ERM/Bank of England, Latin America, Tequila); Niels Kaastrup-Larsen notes that crisis-alpha studies in the trend industry nevertheless start with the tech bubble and ignore them.

corrections.issue: Stated with more certainty than the speaker used. Mark says the convenience yield 'may have disappeared' at the long end and that bill issuance 'may be one reason' to issue bills where the yield is, not that this explains it.
corrections.fix: The convenience yield on long Treasuries may have disappeared and now sits mostly in bills, which may be one reason the Treasury is issuing more bills.

completeness_estimate: 0.80 - the first reader captured the main arguments (French yields, return to normal bond yields, convenience yield, geoeconomic fragmentation, stock-outs, ML crowding) but missed the FIMO/FOMO and buyback points, the performance table, the crisis-first-loss pattern, the supercycle view, the natural-rate and inflation inputs, and the mechanism of ML crowding (same schools, faster adaptation, no secrecy).
